criterion_notes.c1: Fails Criterion 1. Aside from a brief introductory sentence citing secondary reports on high-risk reserve drinking-water systems (which fall under federal jurisdiction; Note 3, p. 205) and a passing mention of a statutory allowance for essential household use (p. 197), the chapter does not examine household or community water supply or sanitation service access. Instead, both substantive sections examine provincial freshwater-resource allocation licensing (First in Time, First in Right) and Crown-Indigenous legislative consultation on British Columbia's Water Sustainability Act (Exclusion Criterion 7: water-resource studies unrelated to household or community service access).
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording vs. narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: This paper passes the plain wording of Criterion 2 (yes) because it examines legal, regulatory, and governance factors — specifically British Columbia's First in Time, First in Right (FITFIR) statutory water-licensing regime, federal-provincial jurisdictional division, and Crown consultation processes under the Water Sustainability Act. However, it fails the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading (no) because the rules and procedures analyzed govern raw surface-water resource abstraction priorities and provincial water-resource lawmaking/consultation rather than a rule-type mechanism (such as eligibility screening, tenure/documentation requirements, tariffs, enforcement, or utility regulation) directly governing household or community water or sanitation service access. Because the paper also fails Criteria 1, 3, 4, and 5, plain_criterion2_decision is still exclude.
criterion_notes.c3: Fails Criterion 3 (E05). This edited-volume book chapter is a narrative socio-legal, historical, and normative policy overview with no reported empirical study design, sampling strategy, data-collection protocol, or analytical methods. Its two short illustrative sections synthesize secondary historical/legal scholarship, publicly posted stakeholder submission letters, and the authors' previously published thesis and policy reports (Simms 2014; Joe et al. 2016/2017; Jollymore et al. 2017), concluding with normative proposals for justice-as-recognition, free prior and informed consent, and watershed co-governance.
criterion_notes.c4: Fails Criterion 4. The chapter reports no empirical outcome measuring household or community water or sanitation service access, connection, availability, continuity, reliability, quantity, affordability, or disconnection. It discusses only historical surface-water abstraction license priority rankings/recognition on streams and First Nations' procedural participation and policy influence in legislative consultations.
criterion_notes.c5: Fails Criterion 5. Although the general population context (Indigenous peoples / First Nations in British Columbia, Canada) and policy topics are described, there is no identifiable empirical study design, primary sample, or household/community service-access outcome.
criterion_notes.c6: Satisfies Criterion 6. Full text is published in English.

evidence_quotes.quote: This chapter documents and analyzes examples of regulatory injustice within British Columbia’s water governance framework by exploring two short case studies.
One of the most controversial topics in British Columbia’s water  governance framework is the system for allocating water rights: First in Time, First in Right (FITFIR).

The ultimate outcome of the provincial– federal clash over reserve water licenses, and of the fact that Indigenous peoples could not apply for their own licenses, was that reserve water rights were often left far down the priority list within the provincial system and were frequently cancelled or overridden by settler water licenses

Aside from a handful of public information and consultation workshops, no additional resources were provided to meaningfully engage Indigenous peoples in the review and discussion of the proposed changes to the legislation.
From publicly available documents, it is unclear how the Province chose to consider First Nations submissions into their changing legislative framework – if at all.
Freshwater allocation in British Columbia embodies historical injustices that are strongly contested by Indigenous communities.

raw_response.exposure: British Columbia's First in Time, First in Right (FITFIR) freshwater resource licensing regime and the provincial consultation process for modernizing the BC Water Sustainability Act
raw_response.outcome: not reported (no household or community water or sanitation service-access outcome; discusses historical surface-water license priority rankings and legislative consultation participation/policy uptake)
raw_response.population_and_sample: Indigenous peoples / First Nations in British Columbia, Canada (no primary empirical sample; summarizes illustrative historical cases such as Lower Similkameen Indian Band and 34 Indigenous consultation submissions from prior reports)
raw_response.rationale: Excluded as E05 (no empirical evidence; also out of scope on service access and outcome). This 2018 book chapter presents a narrative socio-legal, historical, and normative policy overview of Indigenous freshwater governance in British Columbia through two illustrative discussions drawn from secondary historical/legal literature and the authors' prior thesis and policy reports (Simms 2014; Joe et al. 2016/2017; Jollymore et al. 2017), without reporting any empirical study design, data-collection methods, or analytical procedures. Substantively, it also examines provincial surface-water resource allocation licensing (FITFIR) and legislative consultation on the BC Water Sustainability Act rather than household or community drinking-water or sanitation service access (c1=no, c2 narrow=no despite passing plain c2, c4=no, c5=no), so the decision is exclude under both the narrow and plain readings of Criterion 2.
raw_response.study_design: not reported (narrative socio-legal and policy book chapter synthesizing secondary literature and prior reports)
